setupSteps: Quick Start / Manual. The simplest choice. On a stepmill, the steps start slowly at the lowest level; change the level with ▲/▼ or + / −. Level numbers are NOT comparable across brands; pick by effort.
What the screen shows. Time, level, steps per minute (SPM), steps or floors climbed, calories, heart rate, and sometimes METs. On a stepmill, a higher level means the steps move faster.
Programs. Common names: Manual, Interval, Fat Burn, Landmark/Summit (climb a famous building), Heart-Rate Control, Fitness Test. Beginners should use Manual.
Weight and age entry. Enter your real weight and age; calories and heart-rate targets depend on them.

Calories and METs on the console. A rough guide only. In a 1991 study on the StairMaster Gauntlet, the machine's estimated METs overstated actual energy use when people held the handrails. Lean less, trust the screen less.
Heart-rate grips. Hold the pads still and lightly for a reading; use RPE and the talk test as your main guide.

Safety key/clip. Most stepmills use a big red stop button rather than a clip; some models may have a clip or safety sensor (check yours). Pedal steppers have no key because nothing moves unless you push. Note: in the US, some StairMaster 8G Gauntlet units were recalled because the steps could speed up without user input; report any machine that changes speed by itself.
Wipe the handrails, front bar and console.
Wear closed training shoes with laces tucked in. No loose dupatta, saree pallu, long scarf, hanging towel or long track-pant cords near the steps; they can catch in the rolling steps.
Check the steps are stopped. Find the red emergency stop button.
Holding both side rails, step onto the lowest step that sits flat, one foot at a time (follow the machine's "getting on" guide; the StairMaster SM916 manual has one).
Stand tall, feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward, whole foot on the step.
Press Quick Start or Manual. Enter age and weight if asked. The steps start at the lowest speed; start climbing as soon as they move.
Set level 1–3 for the first 2–3 minutes (roughly 24–40 steps per minute on a StairMaster; est., since per-level step rates are not published).
Holding the handles, step onto the lower pedal first, then the other.
Feet hip-width, whole foot on each pedal, heels not hanging off the back.
Set a low resistance. Start stepping slowly with smooth, controlled pushes; do not let the pedal crash to the bottom stop.
Home mini stepper: place it on a non-slip mat, near a wall or sturdy table you can touch for balance; check the hydraulic tension knob is set to a light setting.

steps.title: Start climbing slowly at the lowest level
steps.tempo: lowest speed (about 24–40 steps per minute, est.) for 2–3 minutes.
steps.visualCheck: side – body upright over the feet. Front – feet hip-width, knees in line with toes.

steps.title: Place the whole foot on each step
steps.feel: weight through the middle of the foot and heel, not only the toes.
steps.visualCheck: side – the heel is on the step, not hanging off.

steps.title: Push down through the heel and middle of the foot to rise
steps.feel: buttock and front of thigh working as the leg straightens.
steps.breathing: rhythmic, about one breath every 2–4 steps (est.).
steps.visualCheck: side – the pushing leg straightens almost fully (soft knee, not snapped straight) and the hip opens fully.

steps.title: Lift the other leg to the next step
steps.feel: front of the hip lifting the knee; a full step, not a shuffle.
steps.visualCheck: side – the knee lifts so the foot clears the step edge.

steps.title: Stand tall with a light hand on the rails
steps.feel: hands resting, fingers or palms lightly on the rails, shoulders relaxed.
steps.breathing: talk test passes at moderate effort.
steps.visualCheck: side – trunk upright or leaning only slightly forward from the hips (less than about 30°, est.); elbows soft; you are not hanging on the rails.

steps.title: Look forward, not at your feet
steps.visualCheck: side – ear roughly over the shoulder.

steps.title: Keep the knees in line
steps.feel: knees track over the second toe.
steps.visualCheck: front – knees do not fall in towards each other.

steps.title: Raise the level one at a time to your working effort
steps.breathing: you can talk but not sing (moderate, RPE 5–6/10, Borg 12–13).
steps.tempo: wait about 30–60 seconds after each change before judging (est.).
steps.visualCheck: if you start leaning hard on the rails or taking tiny steps, the level is too high for now.

steps.title: Hold the working pace for the planned time (section 7)
Cool down: 2–3 minutes at the lowest level
Stop the machine before stepping off
steps.feel: legs may feel wobbly for a few seconds. Hold the rail and stand still for a moment before walking away; if dizzy, sit down.

steps.title: Wipe the rails, front bar and console

commonMistakes.title: Leaning on or hanging from the rails
commonMistakes.text: Leaning on or hanging from the rails. It takes body weight off the legs, so the workout gets easier than the screen suggests: oxygen use was significantly lower with handrail support on the StairMaster Gauntlet (Gerhards, 1991 thesis), and up to about 8% lower in women using handrails on a stepping machine (Ohio State study). It also rounds the back and loads the wrists. Fix: lower the level until you can climb with a light touch.

commonMistakes.title: Level too high
commonMistakes.text: Level too high. Common in Indian gyms where people copy the person next to them. Leads to rail-hanging, tiny steps and early exhaustion. Fix: start at level 1–3; increase by one level at a time.

commonMistakes.title: Tiny, shuffling steps or toes only
commonMistakes.text: Tiny, shuffling steps or toes only. Less glute work and more calf strain. Fix: whole foot on each step, push through the heel, straighten the leg at the top.

commonMistakes.title: Hunching over the console / staring at feet or phone
commonMistakes.text: Hunching over the console / staring at feet or phone. Rounds the upper back and neck. Fix: eyes forward; phone on the console shelf or listen instead.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving in
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving in. Strains the inside of the knee. Fix: feet hip-width, knees over the second toe; slow down.

commonMistakes.title: Stepping off a moving stepmill, or getting on while it moves
commonMistakes.text: Stepping off a moving stepmill, or getting on while it moves. A fall hazard. Fix: press Stop, wait for a full stop, hold both rails, step down.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knee hard at the top
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knee hard at the top. Fix: straighten with a soft knee.

commonMistakes.title: Trusting the calorie number
commonMistakes.text: Trusting the calorie number. Console estimates assume you are not holding the rails. Fix: use the MET estimates in section 10.

commonMistakes.title: Too long, too soon
commonMistakes.text: Too long, too soon. Stair climbing gets hard quickly; beginners who try 20–30 minutes often end up sore or hanging on the rails. Fix: start at 5–10 minutes and add 1–2 minutes per session.

safetyNotes: If you have a health condition, check with a doctor or physiotherapist before starting.

Knee problems: stair ascent loads the knee more than level walking. In people with instrumented knee implants, average peak knee forces were about 316% of body weight on stair ascent, 346% on descent and 261% on level walking (Kutzner et al., 2010). A 2024 UK Biobank study (nearly 400,000 people) linked more frequent stair climbing with higher risk of knee osteoarthritis, especially in people genetically prone to it. With knee pain: start slow and short, use a lower step rate, avoid skip-a-step, and choose the bike or elliptical if pain rises.
Low-back problems: stand tall; leaning over the rails rounds the back. Stop if back pain appears.
Balance problems, dizziness, or new to machines: use the rails lightly, start at the slowest level and stand next to the stop button. Get off slowly; legs often feel wobbly after a climb.
High blood pressure or heart disease: moderate effort, longer warm-up and cool-down, no breath-holding, no all-out bursts unless your doctor agrees. The effort rises fast, so monitor RPE closely.

Pregnancy: stair walking becomes less stable in late pregnancy (a 2013 study of 29 pregnant women found changes that may raise fall risk, with more side-to-side sway in the third trimester), and ACOG advises avoiding activities with a high fall risk. If cleared and experienced, keep to slow levels with both hands on the rails, talk-test effort, avoid overheating; switch to the stationary bike as balance changes.
Recent surgery: only with surgeon or physiotherapist clearance.

Stop immediately if: chest pain or pressure; unusual breathlessness; dizziness or feeling faint; irregular or racing heartbeat; sharp knee, hip or ankle pain; loss of balance. Press the stop button first, then step off holding the rails. Seek medical help for chest symptoms.
Spotter: not needed. If you feel unwell, press Stop rather than trying to step off moving stairs.

Hazards: loose clothing, cords or towels can catch in rolling steps; keep children away from the machine; never put a hand on moving steps; report any machine that speeds up by itself (recall precedent: StairMaster 8G Gauntlet, CPSC).

Gym etiquette: stepmills are popular and few in number in most Indian gyms; respect any time limit (often 20–30 min at peak hours, est.), wipe the rails and console, do not leave a towel on it to "reserve" it.
